policy: Review every closed candidate set. Select only when ASV wording or an explicit mapped textual note distinguishes a reading; otherwise mark underdetermined and retain the base fallback. The base candidate is the SBLGNT reading.

decisions.evidence: ASV renders a causal connective before the last clause: 'I would have told you; for I go to prepare a place for you.' The omission leaves 'I go to prepare' asyndetic, with nothing for 'for' to render.
ASV opens the verse 'And if I go and prepare a place for you', rendering the connective the omission drops.
Word order only; 'prepare a place for you' is the same English under either sequence of the pronoun and noun.

The ASV text reads 'ye know the way'; its textual note, 'Many ancient authorities read And whither I go ye know, and the way ye know', puts the longer reading (kai ten hodon oidate) in the margin, so the shorter reading stands in the text.
ASV begins Thomas's question with no connective: 'we know not whither thou goest; how know we the way?' The added kai would surface as 'and how'.
ASV reads 'how know we the way?' with no modal. dunametha ... eidenai would give 'how can we know the way'; the plain indicative oidamen ten hodon is what the ASV renders.
An article whose presence or absence the English does not show; ASV's nouns in 'the way, and the truth, and the life' are articular either way.
ASV's 'If ye had known me' is a pluperfect in a contrary-to-fact protasis, rendering egnokeite, not the perfect egnokate ('if ye have known me').

ASV's 'ye would have known my Father also' is an unreal apodosis with an, which excludes the future gnosesthe ('ye shall know'); it does not distinguish an edeite from egnokeite an, both of which yield 'would have known'.
ASV runs on with a colon and no connective, 'my Father also: from henceforth ye know him'; the added kai would surface as 'and from henceforth'.
English requires an object for these transitive verbs, so 'ye know him, and have seen him' is what the ASV would read whether or not the Greek pronoun is expressed.
Case only: dative and accusative of duration both give ASV's 'so long time'.
ASV reads 'how sayest thou, Show us the Father?' with no connective; the added kai would surface as 'and how sayest thou'.

ASV distinguishes the two verbs: 'the words that I say unto you I speak not from myself.' 'say' renders lego against 'speak' for the following lalo; the lalo reading would put the same verb in both places.
An article the English does not show; ASV reads 'the Father' either way.
ASV reads 'but the Father abiding in me doeth his works', with no resumptive pronoun; the added autos would surface as 'he doeth'.
ASV reads 'doeth his works'; the possessive renders autou, which the omission lacks ('doeth the works').
ASV supplies the object in the second clause: 'or else believe me for the very works' sake.' The 'me' there renders the added moi.
ASV reads 'because I go unto the Father', without the possessive that mou would give ('unto my Father').
The ASV text reads 'If ye shall ask anything in my name' with no object, and its note 'Many ancient authorities add me' assigns me to the margin; the text therefore omits it.
ASV's 'that will I do' has both a fronted object and an expressed subject, but English needs an object for 'do' and a subject pronoun in either case, so it does not settle ego against touto.
ASV reads 'ye will keep my commandments', a future indicative in the apodosis, not the imperative 'keep my commandments' that teresate would give.
ASV reads 'that he may be with you for ever'; 'be' excludes mene ('that he may abide'), but does not distinguish the copula standing here from the same copula placed after 'for ever'.
Placement only: 'that he may be with you for ever' reads identically whether the copula precedes or follows 'for ever'.
English requires an object for the verb, so ASV's 'neither knoweth him' stands whether or not the Greek pronoun is expressed.
ASV sets the clause off with a colon and no adversative: 'neither knoweth him: ye know him'. The added de would surface as 'but ye know him'.
ASV reads 'and shall be in you', a future rendering estai, not the present estin ('and is in you').
Active and middle futures of the same verb; both give ASV's 'ye shall live also'.
Word order only; 'ye shall know' is the same English under either sequence of verb and pronoun.
ASV reads 'Lord, what is come to pass that thou wilt manifest thyself unto us', with no connective before the question; the added kai would surface as 'and what'.
Middle against active of the same verb; ASV's 'make our abode with him' needs the possessive for the English idiom either way, so the voice is not shown.
English needs a subject pronoun for 'said' regardless, so ASV's 'all that I said unto you' does not show whether the emphatic ego stands in the Greek.
ASV's 'Ye heard how I said to you' renders a single verb of speaking after the connective and does not show a second one; the English cannot be traced to one reading rather than the other.
ASV reads 'for the Father is greater than I', without the possessive that mou would give ('my Father').
ASV's periphrasis 'as the Father gave me commandment' renders the noun-plus-verb entolen edoken; eneteilato would give the single verb 'commanded me'.
